analysis.one_liner: Raises fines and prison terms for companies caught illegally employing children and requires a public report on violators.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 42 Democratic cosponsors in April 2023, but the House Education and the Workforce Committee never acted on it and it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the federal child labor rules to make violations much more expensive and risky for employers. Companies caught illegally employing minors would face civil fines ranging from $1,000 up to $700,000 per violation, and owners or managers who willfully or repeatedly break the law could be prosecuted, facing fines up to $100,000 and prison terms of up to 5 years — or up to $500,000 and 10 years if a child worker is seriously hurt or killed. It would also require the Labor Department to publish an annual public report naming employers that violated child labor laws and listing goods made with illegal child labor. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any action after being sent to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 18 who work, or could be pushed into illegal work, would gain stronger protection: fines for violations would go up roughly tenfold, willful or repeat violators could face criminal prosecution including prison, and violations causing a minor's death could bring $700,000 fines (doubled for repeat offenders) and up to 10 years in prison. Consumers and the public would also gain an annual public report naming violators and the goods made with illegal child labor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minors working illegally in the US

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum civil penalty for illegally employing a minor from $11,000 to a range of $1,000 to $150,000, and raises the maximum from $11,000 to $150,000 — doubled to $300,000 for repeated or willful violations.

Raises the penalty for violations that seriously injure or kill a minor to $20,000–$700,000, and creates a new $70,000–$700,000 penalty range for violations that kill a child worker, both subject to doubling for repeat or willful offenders.

Creates criminal penalties for willful or repeated child labor violations: up to a $100,000 fine and 5 years in prison, rising to a $500,000 fine and 10 years in prison if a worker under 18 dies or is seriously injured.

Requires the Labor Department to publish an annual report naming employers that violated child labor laws, listing the goods made with illegal child labor (including consumer-facing brands), and summarizing violation trends, enforcement efforts, and data gaps.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that violate child labor laws would pay sharply higher fines, and owners or managers who willfully break the law could face prison time. Businesses would also see violations named publicly in an annual government report.

drawbacks.text: Higher penalties can fall hardest on small, low-margin employers that make paperwork mistakes rather than on large violators, since the same civil fine applies regardless of company size.

The bill adds enforcement and reporting requirements without adding funding, so more severe penalties may not translate into more inspections unless Congress separately appropriates money — the report itself is directed to state what resources would be needed.

The bill is narrow: it raises penalties and requires reporting but does not change which jobs minors may legally hold, so it would not address the legal loopholes some states have been loosening around teen work hours and hazardous occupations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted at a real and growing problem: child labor violations rose sharply in the early 2020s, and the existing federal fines — as low as about $11,000 — are widely regarded as too small to deter large companies. Higher fines, possible prison time, and a public list of violators would give regulators real leverage. The main costs fall on violators, not the public, though smaller businesses making honest mistakes could face the same large fines as big firms, and the bill does not fund more inspectors to find violations in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 27, 2023, amending the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 to raise child labor penalties and require an annual public report on violations.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote are recorded in the bill's action history.
The bill ended the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 without receiving a vote, so it would need to be reintroduced to have any effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who use illegal child labor are better off, since the higher fines and criminal exposure it would have created never became law. The bill's 42 Democratic cosponsors also gained a platform for the issue but saw no policy change.

for.name: Rep. Daniel Kildee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with 35 initial colleagues in April 2023.

for.name: House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors, all Democrats, growing the bill's support to 42 members, none of whom chaired the committee with jurisdiction over it.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.role: House Committee on Education and the Workforce (Republican majority)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or floor vote from its referral on April 27, 2023 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill was referred to a committee run by the House Republican majority, which took no action on it before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Employers that use child labor, including meatpacking, agriculture, and food service firms that have been cited for violations
industries.note: These are the employers whose illegal child labor would draw fines up to $700,000 per violation and possible prison terms for willful violations under the bill. Stronger penalties and public naming would raise the cost of doing business for them.

industries.industry: Law-abiding employers in the same sectors
industries.note: The bill is enforcement-based, so compliant businesses would face no new costs and would not gain a subsidy or locked-in market role; it mainly raises the price of breaking the law.
